first_impression.reaction: Okay, this is actually about my search. First line tells me it's two documents, and it's dated October 2026, so I don't have to wonder if it's some 2019 post. The bit about other guides being written for Brits and Americans made me trust it more, because that's exactly what I kept getting on Google. I read the Key Takeaways, then jumped straight to costs, then skimmed the timeline and FAQ.

journey.quote: Most guides online are written for British or American couples and talk about a Certificate of No Impediment, which Italy will not accept from you.
journey.reaction: Yes. That's the exact confusion I had. Tells me this one is actually for Australians.

journey.quote: This is the Australian version, as at October 2026: what to prepare at home, what to sign in Rome or Milan, what happens at the town hall, and where the marriage stands once you are home.
journey.reaction: Dated, and it tells me what's coming. Is this still true in 2026? It says so. Good.

journey.quote: Australians need two documents to marry in Italy: an Atto Notorio from the Italian consulate for your state, and a Nulla Osta sworn in person at the Australian Embassy in Rome or the Consulate-General in Milan.
journey.reaction: That's my answer, in the first screen on my phone. If I left now I'd still have got what I came for.

journey.quote: Get it before you leave, from the Italian consulate for the state where you live.
journey.reaction: Hang on, I'm Australian but I don't live in an Australian state right now. Which consulate do I use then? Melbourne even wants proof of address in Victoria or Tasmania. Not answered.

journey.section: Step by step once you arrive in Italy
journey.quote: Rome's Prefettura legalisation office opens four mornings a week, and some comuni want your declaration three days before the wedding, so allow a working week rather than arriving two days out.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of practical line I actually need. A working week. I can plan leave around that.

journey.quote: The squeeze is in the middle. Both documents expire six months after signing, so a date that moves late can mean signing again.
journey.reaction: Useful warning. But I still don't know when I should start the whole thing. Twelve months out? Six? The takeaways never say.

journey.quote: Most official steps carry a fee, and amounts move with exchange rates or annual indexation.
journey.reaction: Just tell me how much it costs. I came to this section for numbers and there isn't a single one.

journey.quote: a consular fee applies, set by each consulate's tariff.
journey.reaction: Every bullet says 'a fee applies'. I knew that. A rough figure with a date on it would do.

journey.quote: Not published: interpreter and translation rates. Your Wedded Advisor costs the full paperwork in AUD for your comune.
journey.reaction: Feels like the price is being held back so I have to enquire. Maybe that's not the intent, but that's how it reads after five fee-less bullets.

journey.quote: On Sydney's list, two Australians with two certificates and two translations each can need eight apostilles.
journey.reaction: Eight! Good to know, and it makes the missing per-apostille fee more annoying, because now I want to multiply it.

journey.section: Is an Italian marriage recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here.
journey.reaction: Clear, quoted from the government. That was my next question and the heading matched it.

journey.quote: No. The Embassy says Certificates of No Impediment are not valid for use in Italy.
journey.reaction: Short, direct FAQ answers. This is what I'd screenshot.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor confirms the comune's list in writing.
journey.reaction: I don't know who Wedded Advisor is yet and it keeps popping up at the end of sections. Once is fine; by the fifth time it feels like a sales nudge.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how much does the paperwork cost in total, even as a ballpark in AUD, as at 2026?
What does the Nulla Osta fee or a single DFAT apostille actually cost?
Which Italian consulate do I use if I'm Australian but living overseas (e.g. in Singapore)?
How many months before the wedding should I start the whole process?
How far ahead do Rome and Milan release Nulla Osta appointments?

turn_offs_found.quote: Most official steps carry a fee, and amounts move with exchange rates or annual indexation.
turn_offs_found.why: The cost heading matches my question but the section has no numbers. That's the answer being buried, just in a different way.

turn_offs_found.quote: For getting married in Italy from Australia, the dates that matter are set by the documents.
turn_offs_found.why: The timeline is a ten-row, three-column table. On my phone on the train that's a lot of sideways scrolling. Good content, hard to read in that format.

would_share_with: My partner, specifically the Key Takeaways and FAQ
A friend planning a wedding in Italy who is also Australian

cta_reaction.quote: A Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD and stays with you from the first document to the last dance.
cta_reaction.why: Not today. I came for an answer and got most of it, so I'd bookmark the page rather than talk to anyone. 'Quotes in AUD' is nice, but I'd want to see a rough cost on the page before I'd hand over my details. Maybe later when we've picked a date.

top_3_changes: Put actual fee figures (or ranges) with an 'as at' date in the costs section, at least for the Nulla Osta, a DFAT apostille and the Atto Notorio, so 'What the paperwork costs' answers the question in its heading.
Add one Key Takeaway on when to start, e.g. how many months before the wedding to begin the documents, since the takeaways cover what and where but not when.
Say what Australians living outside Australia should do about the Atto Notorio, since every option given assumes you live in an Australian state.
